props.title: Baby's Laxative

sections.content: **Baby's Laxative (1931)** (1931) stands as a fascinating early example of pre-Code Hollywood comedy pushing boundaries with taboo subjects. This rare Hal Roach short film, largely forgotten today, demonstrates how early sound-era comedies tackled domestic situations with surprising frankness. Like other daring pre-Code films like Night Nurse (1931) and The Smiling Lieutenant (1931), it represents a brief window of creative freedom before the strict enforcement of the Production Code in 1934.

sections.content: The film's approach to bodily functions and medicinal themes connects it to other early sound comedies that tested censorship boundaries. **Min and Bill** (1930) and **Politics** (1931) similarly used physical comedy and domestic situations to push the envelope. The short's director, Robert McGowan, was known for helming many Our Gang/Little Rascals comedies, bringing his experience with child actors to this more controversial territory. SUBHEAD: Pre-Code Hollywood Context

Pre-Code Hollywood regularly addressed taboo subjects before censorship crackdown. **Safe in Hell** (1931) dealt with prostitution, **The Story of Temple Drake** (1933) tackled rape, and **Baby Face** (1933) showed a woman sleeping her way to the top. **Baby's Laxative** (1931), while a comedy, fits into this broader context of films that wouldn't have been possible just a few years later.
